docs.text: Your friend is right to question the hype; recent data suggests AI coding tools can actually slow developers down. A study by the nonprofit METR found that when engineers use AI, they take 19% longer to complete tasks. This contradicts developer expectations, as many believed AI would speed them up by roughly 24%. Even after experiencing this slowdown, users still overestimated the benefits, believing they had gained a 20% boost. However, there are important caveats. The study notes these results may reflect current technological limits rather than a permanent flaw. Furthermore, experts warn that recent job market struggles and layoffs are likely driven more by broader economic slowdowns and companies seeking to stay lean, rather than AI directly replacing engineers. While AI can write code, challenges remain when dealing with complex logic or large-scale development. Ultimately, while the technology is powerful, it hasn't yet delivered the full promise of automation expected in the industry.

Yes, according to a new METR study of 16 experienced developers working on complex projects. Developers estimated that AI had sped them up by about 20%, but measurements showed it had slowed them down by about 20%. A METR researcher said the result surprised the AI community. The likely explanation is that current LLMs often cannot give the exact answer in one shot, so back-and-forth prompting can take longer than writing the code. One participant called LLMs a dopamine shortcut button. Caveats: the study covers only experienced coders, not newcomers who might benefit more, developers are still learning how to use these tools, and the authors urge readers not to overgeneralize.

Yes, but only in one narrow study. The nonprofit METR ran a randomized trial with 16 experienced open-source developers doing 246 real tasks on large, mature codebases they knew well. When AI was allowed, mostly Cursor Pro with Claude, tasks took 19 percent longer. The striking part is perception: developers expected AI to save them 24 percent of their time, and even after being slowed down, they believed it had saved them about 20 percent. Economists and machine learning experts had also predicted big gains. The authors warn against overgeneralizing. The study covers early-2025 tools and experienced developers on familiar, huge repositories. It doesn't mean AI tools never help, and earlier studies on simpler, isolated tasks found real speedups.

Yes, in one rigorous study. METR ran a randomized controlled trial with 16 experienced open-source developers completing 246 real tasks on mature repositories averaging over a million lines of code. When AI tools such as Cursor Pro with Claude were allowed, tasks took 19% longer. The developers had predicted a 24% speedup and still believed afterward that AI had sped them up by 20%, so the perception gap is large. They accepted under 44% of AI suggestions and often reworked the code. Caveats: the sample was small, the tools were early-2025 versions, and the work was on large codebases the developers already knew well. The researchers say this does not mean AI tools never help. Other studies that found gains used simpler, more isolated tasks.

The measurements showed it had slowed them down by about 20 percent. The likely reason is that today's models often can't read exactly what a developer wants in one shot, so they need lots of back-and-forth, which can take longer than writing the code yourself. The authors urge caution: the study only covers experienced coders, who may gain less than newcomers, and developers are still learning how to use these tools. Your friend is right to question the hype; a recent randomized study actually found that AI coding tools made experienced developers slower, not faster. While participants predicted a 24% speedup, they were clocked at being 19% slower on average. This counterintuitive result stems from several factors: over-optimism about AI's utility, the fact that highly familiar developers didn't need much help, and the tools' struggle with large codebases. Developers spent more time prompting, waiting, and reviewing flawed outputs than actually coding. However, it is crucial to note the study's key caveats. The authors warn these findings are specific to their experimental conditions—specifically involving experienced devs working on massive repositories. They explicitly state this doesn't mean AI is universally useless or that future models won't improve. In different settings, such as smaller projects or for junior developers, AI might still offer significant benefits. So, while it slowed down this specific group right now, the tool's effectiveness depends heavily on context and user experience.

Your friend is right to question the hype; recent rigorous research suggests AI coding tools can actually slow experienced programmers down. A comprehensive study by Model Evaluation & Threat Research (METR) found that seasoned developers took 19% longer to complete tasks when using popular AI assistants like Cursor Pro and Claude compared to working without them. This contradicts the common belief that AI boosts speed, revealing a significant gap between perception and reality: while developers predicted a 24% time reduction, they still felt 20% more productive after experiencing the slowdown themselves. The study highlights that this friction occurs because experienced coders often reject most AI suggestions (less than 44%) and spend considerable time reviewing and modifying generated code to fit complex, mature codebases. While earlier studies using simple tasks showed speed gains, real-world scenarios involving intricate dependencies reveal a different story. The key takeaway is that organizations should not mistake developer satisfaction for actual productivity. Instead of treating AI as a universal accelerator, it should be used contextually—augmenting cognition for documentation or boilerplate while relying on human expertise for complex logic and codebase familiarity.

When AI tools were allowed, mainly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5 or 3.7 Sonnet, developers took 19% longer. They had expected a 24% speedup, and afterward they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%, which is the striking part. Key caveats apply. The participants were experienced developers working on codebases they knew well, and the repositories were very large, so the results may not hold in other settings. The study's authors also say the results do not necessarily spell doom for AI coding tools. Developers accepted less than 44% of AI suggestions and often reworked the output. Other studies, using simpler and more isolated tasks, found real gains, such as 26% more tasks completed with GitHub Copilot. So AI can slow down experienced developers on complex work, but it is not a universal rule.
